Name: cross_lingual_refusal_direction
Title: One Refusal to Rule Them All? Cross-Lingual Structure of the Safety-Refusal Direction
Short Hypothesis: Safety refusal is mediated by a largely shared refusal direction across languages, but its magnitude and threshold are language-specific and weaker in low-resource languages, mechanistically explaining cross-lingual jailbreak vulnerability; aligning the shared direction's threshold across languages closes the gap.
Related Work: Refusal-direction work (Arditi et al.) is English-centric; multilingual jailbreak studies (Yong et al. low-resource jailbreaks) are behavioral. We connect the two: a shared refusal direction with language-varying threshold explains multilingual safety gaps, and we test threshold equalization as a mechanistic fix.
Abstract: Multilingual models are more easily jailbroken in low-resource languages, a serious safety gap. We hypothesize a mechanistic cause: refusal is mediated by a mostly shared refusal direction in the residual stream, but the effective activation threshold for triggering refusal is language-specific and lower (weaker) in low-resource languages, so harmful prompts fail to cross it. We extract refusal directions per language from harmful/harmless contrast pairs, measure their cross-lingual similarity, and estimate per-language refusal-trigger thresholds. We predict high directional overlap but systematically lower refusal activation in low-resource languages on matched harmful prompts. Causally, we test whether adding the shared refusal direction (or lowering the threshold) in low-resource languages restores refusal without harming helpfulness, and whether the same jailbreak that bypasses low-resource refusal maps to sub-threshold activation. Metrics: cross-lingual refusal-direction cosine similarity, per-language refusal activation on matched harmful prompts, jailbreak success vs activation, and refusal-restoration rate under intervention. This provides a mechanistic account of multilingual safety disparities and a direction-level mitigation.
Experiments: Extract refusal directions per language from harmful/harmless contrast pairs (matched, translated).
Measure cross-lingual cosine similarity of refusal directions.
Estimate per-language refusal activation on matched harmful prompts; relate to resource level.
Correlate jailbreak success with sub-threshold refusal activation across languages.
Causal fix: add shared refusal direction / equalize threshold in low-resource languages; measure refusal restoration and helpfulness retention.
Test whether known low-resource jailbreaks correspond to reduced activation.
Controls: over-refusal check on benign prompts; random-direction addition.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Working with harmful prompts requires careful safety handling; use established red-team sets responsibly.
Translated harmful prompts may be lower quality in low-resource languages, confounding activation.
Refusal is multi-component; a single direction may be incomplete.
Interventions risk over-refusal; helpfulness trade-off must be measured.
